analysis.one_liner: Sets enforceable standards for immigration detention and phases out private for-profit detention facilities.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 135 House Democrats and no Republicans, sits in two House subcommittees with no vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set binding standards for every facility holding immigrants for the Department of Homeland Security, require unannounced inspections by the department's independent inspector general, and fine or shut down facilities that repeatedly fail. It would end solitary confinement in immigration detention, require a hearing before an immigration judge within 48 hours of most arrests, presume release unless the government can prove detention is necessary, and ban detention of anyone under 18. It would also phase out, over three years, all contracts with private, for-profit detention companies and require that detention facilities be owned by the government.
analysis.who_benefits: Immigrants held in DHS custody and their families: they would gain enforceable living conditions, unannounced independent inspections, prompt court hearings on whether they must be held, a legal presumption of release, access to counsel in private, an end to solitary confinement, and protection from detention for children and defined vulnerable people, such as pregnant women and survivors of torture. Communities would gain a public website listing every facility, its population, and its compliance record, plus 24-hour notice of any death in custody with a public root-cause report.

how_it_helps.text: The Homeland Security Secretary must write detention standards meeting the American Bar Association's civil immigration detention standards within one year, and update them at least every two years.

The Inspector General must inspect every detention facility in person, unannounced, at least annually, publish each report online within 60 days, and can require fines starting at 10 percent of a contract's value or termination of the contract after repeated failures.
Any death of a person in DHS custody must be reported to Congress within 24 hours, investigated with a root-cause analysis, and explained in a public report within 60 days.
Detained people who are injured by violations of the standards could sue in federal court for damages and injunctions, with attorney fees available.

Most arrested immigrants would get a hearing before an immigration judge within 48 hours on whether detention is justified, with a presumption of release the government must overcome with clear and convincing evidence, and no one could be held solely for being unable to pay bond.
No one under 18 could be held in an ICE facility, and solitary confinement would be banned outright.

Within three years, DHS could no longer contract with for-profit companies to run detention facilities or electronic monitoring, and all detention facilities would have to be owned and operated by the government.

analysis.who_pays: Private prison and detention companies, which would lose their DHS contracts over three years, and companies selling electronic monitoring such as ankle monitors, which would be barred from the alternatives-to-detention program. Taxpayers would bear the cost of building and running government-owned detention facilities and a community-based case management program, and immigration enforcement would be constrained because detention would become the exception requiring court justification rather than the default.

drawbacks.text: Ending for-profit contracts within three years would leave a gap between the closure of private facilities and available government-owned bed space, likely requiring expensive new construction and forcing detainee transfers, and could strain capacity during enforcement surges.

The presumption of release, 48-hour probable-cause hearings, and limits on using arrests alone to justify detention would make it harder to hold people pending removal, which supporters of stricter enforcement argue would let people who would not show up for court return to the community.
A ban on solitary confinement in all cases, including for people accused of violence against other detainees, removes a management tool prisons of every kind currently use.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives detained immigrants enforceable rights and real oversight of facilities that today are largely inspected on the government's own terms, at the cost of a large, disruptive restructuring of the detention system. The strongest honest objections are the transition cost and capacity risk of ending private contracts on a three-year clock, and the release presumption, which shifts detention from a default to something the government must justify case by case.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in early December 2025 and sent to the House Judiciary and Homeland Security Committees, where both sent it to subcommittees; no vote has been scheduled.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 3, 2025, and referred to the House Judiciary Committee and the House Homeland Security Committee.

The next day, the bill was referred to the Homeland Security Subcommittee on Border Security and Enforcement and the Judiciary Subcommittee on Oversight, Investigations, and Accountability, where it has sat since.
The bill has 135 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, and no Republican cosponsors.
Republicans hold the House majority in the 119th Congress, and no further action has been taken on the bill since the subcommittee referrals.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private detention and electronic monitoring companies, which keep their existing DHS contracts because the phase-out has not moved. Detained immigrants see no change in conditions or due process. The bill's backers retain a fully built proposal on the record but have no mechanism to advance it in this Congress.

for.name: Rep. Pramila Jayapal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 135 House cosponsors for it.

for.name: 135 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors within days of introduction; no Republican did.

sides.party_line_note: All 135 cosponsors are Democrats; the bill drew no Republican support, and the Republican House majority has taken no action on it since referring it to subcommittees.

industries.industry: Private, for-profit detention contractors (companies running immigrant detention facilities for DHS)
industries.note: The bill would bar DHS from contracting with for-profit detention operators and terminate all such contracts within three years, ending a multibillion-dollar revenue stream. These companies profit per detainee day, so their financial interest runs directly against reducing detention and improving conditions.

The bill would end for-profit contracts for alternatives-to-detention monitoring and bar ankle monitors from the replacement program, and would prohibit charging immigrants fees to participate. These firms currently bill the government, and sometimes the monitored person, for surveillance.

industries.industry: Community-based nonprofits and case management organizations
industries.note: The bill directs DHS to run a community-based case management program and gives contracting priority to nonprofits experienced with immigrant and refugee services. They would gain a government-funded service role as detention shrinks.

Because all detention would have to be in government-owned facilities, DHS and public facility operators would gain buildings, staff, and budget, while being subject to binding standards, unannounced inspections, and fines they do not face today.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, a Republican House majority, and the bill sitting in both committees' subcommittees since December 4, the most likely path is that it stays there for the rest of the 119th Congress without a hearing, markup, or floor vote. Similar detention standards and private-prison phase-out bills from the same sponsor have not advanced under divided or Republican control.
